pages.text:
Carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites are widely used in lightweight aerospace, automotive, and wind-energy structures
owing to their high specific strength and stiffness and durability. However, dissimilar bonding is highly sensitive to surface conditions:
CFRP surfaces exhibit low surface energy and may retain mold-release agents, and conventional pretreatments have limitations in control-
ling and homogenizing surface topography and chemical activation, which undermines interfacial adhesion and reliability. This work pre-
sents a 355 nm flat-top picosecond-laser approach that integrates bioinspired hierarchical texturing with surface activation, enabling
programmable construction of tree-frog–inspired “plateau-connected-groove” patterns and concomitantly enhancing surface polarity.
Roughness and feature depth increase with fluence; the water contact angle decreases to 8.0°; and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicates
higher fractions of oxidized carbon species, while the Raman I_D/I_G ratio remains essentially unchanged. In AA7075/CFRP single-lap-
shear tests, the lap-shear strength increases from 5.9 to 19.6 MPa at 5.8 J cm−2, accompanied by a transition from interfacial adhesive failure
to fiber-dominated mixed failure. Mechanistically, at an appropriate fluence, hierarchical micro-/nanostructures, together with enhanced
surface polarity, enable synergistic mechanical interlocking and chemical coupling; by contrast, excessive fluence can introduce voids and
microcracks and promote partial Cassie wetting. The non-contact, programmable process is compatible with complex geometries and auto-
mation, providing a high-throughput surface-engineering route for durable joining in CFRP–Al lap joints and stiffeners in aircraft, bonds
between CFRP skins and aluminum honeycomb/cores; mixed-material joints in automotive body structures, and wind-turbine blade root–
insert interfaces.

However, to the best of our knowledge, no systematic study has
investigated laser surface treatment or (bioinspired) texturing of
CFRP using a flat-top beam. Considering that the resin and carbon
fibers in CFRP differ markedly in ablation threshold and thermal
properties—differences that amplify the spatial nonuniformity of
Gaussian beams, a 355 nm flat-top picosecond laser that simultane-
ously textures and activates CFRP surfaces is used to build a bioins-
pired “plateau-connected-groove” polygonal pattern derived from
tree-frog toe pads, to enhance hydrophilicity. Fluence-dependent
morphology, wettability, and chemistry are systematically mapped
and correlated with AA7075/CFRP lap-shear performance. The
process
yields
hierarchical
micro-/nanotopographies,
increases
surface polarity without degrading graphitic integrity, and drives a
failure-mode transition from interfacial adhesion to fiber-dominated
co-failure. Compared with Gaussian-based approaches, the flat-top
profile widens the processing window and improves reproducibility.
These results provide a high-throughput, automation-ready route for
durable multi-material joining of CFRP components.

The CFRP used in this study employed an epoxy resin matrix
reinforced with SYT49S plain-weave carbon fiber fabric, where
both the warp and fill yarns are 12 K carbon fiber yarns, composed
of 12 000 individual carbon filaments. The single fiber diameter of
the T700 SYT49S is 7 μm, and therefore, the diameter of the 12 K
carbon fiber yarn is approximately 0.3– 0.4 mm. The structural
adhesive was SW-9, an ambient-curing adhesive. Prior to surface
treatment, CFRP specimens were ultrasonically cleaned for 10 min,
rinsed with anhydrous alcohol, and air-dried. Single-lap-shear
specimens prepared in accordance with GB/T 7124-2008 are shown
in Fig. 1(a); each measured 100 × 25 mm with a thickness of
1.6 mm. The bonding schematic is provided in Fig. 1(b). CFRP and
AA7075 substrates were bonded with an epoxy adhesive both
before and after surface treatment, with a bonding area of
25 × 12.5 mm2. Except for laser texturing applied to the CFRP, the
AA7075 surface was sanded to remove oxides and increase rough-
ness. Untreated CFRP and aluminum alloy were used as reference
samples.

Although laser processing has been widely applied in micro-
fabrication and surface-quality control, current processes predomi-
nantly rely on Gaussian beams, whose steep fluence gradients
readily induce overprocessing at the center and underprocessing at
the edges, thereby narrowing the process window and undermining
consistency and repeatability. Shaping the beam into a flat-top
(top-hat) profile can significantly improve spatial energy unifor-
mity, reduce the heat-affected zone (HAZ) and process variability,
and such advantages are well documented in prior studies across
multiple material systems: achieving high-consistency, low-damage,
high-aspect-ratio through-silicon via (TSV) drilling in Si;19 attenu-
ating elemental segregation and suppressing Laves-phase formation
in Inconel 718 during laser-based deposition/melting,20 and in
laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) promoting stable, directional epi-
taxial growth with a widened process window21 forming homoge-
neous nano-/micro-structures and ultra-smooth surfaces on Ti and
GaN;22,23 significantly reducing laser-induced damage (LID) in
solar cells;24 and, via vector flat-top-beam shaping based on polari-
zation
singularities,
achieving
efficient,
controllable
material
removal and cleaning in comparative process studies.25,26 For
polymer–matrix composites, adjustable flat-top rectangular beams

Building on the strength gains and fracture-surface evidence,
Fig. 13 clarifies how biomimetic structuring enhances the AA7075/
CFRP interface in a fluence-dependent manner. Biomimetic
micro-/nanotopographies promote deeper adhesive penetration
into the CFRP, improving mechanical interlocking and stress trans-
fer. At low fluence, shallow features limit infiltration and interlock-
ing, yielding weak interfaces. At an optimal fluence, well-defined
hierarchical textures enable maximum penetration and robust
anchoring, consistent with the increased lap-shear strength and the
failure-mode transition in Fig. 12. At excessive fluence, voids/
microcracks and disrupted interfacial continuity can reduce the
effective bonding area and introduce stress concentrators, thereby
degrading strength.

In this work, a 355 nm flat-top (top-hat) picosecond laser was
employed to realize integrated biomimetic texturing and surface
activation
of
CFRP.
A
tree-frog–inspired
polygonal
“plateau-connected-groove” pattern was programmed onto the lam-
inate with minimal heat-affected impact. Relative to the pristine
surface (Sa ≈1 μm), laser processing markedly amplified surface
topography (Sa up to ≈39.5 μm) and established hierarchical
roughness
comprising
continuous
boundary
grooves
and
scan-induced ridges. Wettability was substantially improved (the
water contact angle decreased from 81.0° to a minimum of 8.0°).
XPS revealed increased oxygenated functional groups (CZO/
CvO), while Raman I_D/I_G remained essentially unchanged,
indicating enhanced polarity without the degradation of the carbon
framework. Consequently, AA7075/CFRP single-lap-shear strength
increased from 5.9 to 19.6 MPa at 5.8 J cm−2, accompanied by a
transition from interfacial adhesive failure to fiber-dominated
mixed failure. The performance gains are attributed to the synergy
between hierarchical micro-/nanostructures, which promote three-
dimensional mechanical interlocking and adhesive infiltration, and
elevated surface polarity, which enhances wetting and chemical
coupling. The proposed non-contact, computer-controlled flat-top
laser route scales to curved parts and automation, enabling durable
CFRP multimaterial joints in aircraft (CFRP–Al lap joints/string-
ers) and automotive body structures (CFRP skin–honeycomb
bonding/repairs).

paragraphs.text:
Carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites are widely used in lightweight aerospace, automotive, and wind-energy structures
owing to their high specific strength and stiffness and durability. However, dissimilar bonding is highly sensitive to surface conditions:
CFRP surfaces exhibit low surface energy and may retain mold-release agents, and conventional pretreatments have limitations in control-
ling and homogenizing surface topography and chemical activation, which undermines interfacial adhesion and reliability. This work pre-
sents a 355 nm flat-top picosecond-laser approach that integrates bioinspired hierarchical texturing with surface activation, enabling
programmable construction of tree-frog–inspired “plateau-connected-groove” patterns and concomitantly enhancing surface polarity.
Roughness and feature depth increase with fluence; the water contact angle decreases to 8.0°; and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicates
higher fractions of oxidized carbon species, while the Raman I_D/I_G ratio remains essentially unchanged. In AA7075/CFRP single-lap-
shear tests, the lap-shear strength increases from 5.9 to 19.6 MPa at 5.8 J cm−2, accompanied by a transition from interfacial adhesive failure
to fiber-dominated mixed failure. Mechanistically, at an appropriate fluence, hierarchical micro-/nanostructures, together with enhanced
surface polarity, enable synergistic mechanical interlocking and chemical coupling; by contrast, excessive fluence can introduce voids and
microcracks and promote partial Cassie wetting. The non-contact, programmable process is compatible with complex geometries and auto-
mation, providing a high-throughput surface-engineering route for durable joining in CFRP–Al lap joints and stiffeners in aircraft, bonds
between CFRP skins and aluminum honeycomb/cores; mixed-material joints in automotive body structures, and wind-turbine blade root–
insert interfaces.

Building on the strength gains and fracture-surface evidence,
Fig. 13 clarifies how biomimetic structuring enhances the AA7075/
CFRP interface in a fluence-dependent manner. Biomimetic
micro-/nanotopographies promote deeper adhesive penetration
into the CFRP, improving mechanical interlocking and stress trans-
fer. At low fluence, shallow features limit infiltration and interlock-
ing, yielding weak interfaces. At an optimal fluence, well-defined
hierarchical textures enable maximum penetration and robust
anchoring, consistent with the increased lap-shear strength and the
failure-mode transition in Fig. 12. At excessive fluence, voids/
microcracks and disrupted interfacial continuity can reduce the
effective bonding area and introduce stress concentrators, thereby
degrading strength.

paragraphs.text:
In this work, a 355 nm flat-top (top-hat) picosecond laser was
employed to realize integrated biomimetic texturing and surface
activation
of
CFRP.
A
tree-frog–inspired
polygonal
“plateau-connected-groove” pattern was programmed onto the lam-
inate with minimal heat-affected impact. Relative to the pristine
surface (Sa ≈1 μm), laser processing markedly amplified surface
topography (Sa up to ≈39.5 μm) and established hierarchical
roughness
comprising
continuous
boundary
grooves
and
scan-induced ridges. Wettability was substantially improved (the
water contact angle decreased from 81.0° to a minimum of 8.0°).
XPS revealed increased oxygenated functional groups (CZO/
CvO), while Raman I_D/I_G remained essentially unchanged,
indicating enhanced polarity without the degradation of the carbon
framework. Consequently, AA7075/CFRP single-lap-shear strength
increased from 5.9 to 19.6 MPa at 5.8 J cm−2, accompanied by a
transition from interfacial adhesive failure to fiber-dominated
mixed failure. The performance gains are attributed to the synergy
between hierarchical micro-/nanostructures, which promote three-
dimensional mechanical interlocking and adhesive infiltration, and
elevated surface polarity, which enhances wetting and chemical
coupling. The proposed non-contact, computer-controlled flat-top
laser route scales to curved parts and automation, enabling durable
CFRP multimaterial joints in aircraft (CFRP–Al lap joints/string-
ers) and automotive body structures (CFRP skin–honeycomb
bonding/repairs).
